title: Samantha:
headline: Her group was reading a book about censorship when one of their own books got pulled. The faraway idea happened to them, and it became a beautiful conversation.
story: The story of the year at WCCW: the ILP readers were reading The Book Censor's Library at the same time one of the books was pulled from them by the institution. The idea in the book stopped being far away, and it brought the book “really to the forefront”.
Keep eyes on the book and the idea. It is not about the facility and not about what could happen to her. Calm, curious, a little wry. It ends on “a neat experience, as frustrating as it was.”

Machine transcript of P1055419.MOV (Samantha, ILP judge, Washington Corrections Center for Women). Times are mm:ss.s in the file. Speaker labels in the source are often wrong: the questions are the interviewer, the answers are Samantha. “Adenon” is the transcript's spelling of the book Ædnan.

[00:02.5] Alright, so can you introduce yourself and tell us about your relationship with reading? [do not use: interviewer]
[00:08.5] [do not use: she says her full name here; first names only, line left out]
[00:11.5] My relationship with reading has existed since I was a kid, you know?
[00:17.5] I've always had the ability to kind of expand my thinking and show me things that I don't see, even when they're right in front of me.
[00:25.5] Helps me to kind of look at the world through many, many different lenses.
[00:30.5] And also the escapist aspect of it.
[00:34.5] Reading can kind of take me outside of whatever pain I might be experiencing better than anything else.
[00:40.5] So reading is very, very important to me.
[00:43.5] Absolutely.
[00:47.9] Can you walk me through how the conversations about the books unfold? [do not use: interviewer]
[00:53.6] The conversations about these books that we have been reading together, I've actually had a lot of experiences with people who sat down and we talked in the day room with people who weren't reading them.
[01:06.6] And they became very, very interested in the work that we were doing.
[01:10.6] The conversations that we had in this group setting, it's really refreshing to be in a space with like-minded people who are able to see what an author is saying
[01:22.0] and then kind of figure out why are they saying that?
[01:24.6] Why are they saying it in the way that it's being described?
[01:27.7] Because not everybody reads that way.
[01:29.7] A lot of people, which is fine, I think read just for entertainment's sake.
[01:33.6] And reading has so much more to offer that.
[01:35.7] And so being in a space like this with the Freedom Reads Project and being able to actually have conversations about why things are being written in the way that they're being written has been really good.
[01:45.4] Absolutely.
[01:46.3] That was great.
[01:49.7] What new ideas or perspectives have stayed with you from your reading? [do not use: interviewer]
[01:54.8] New ideas or perspectives that have stayed with me I would say the censorship aspect for this group and this event.
[02:05.8] [do not use: hard rule, line left out]
[02:08.8] This group specifically, I think it was really poignant that we were reading a book about censorship at the same time that one of the books got pulled from our content by the institution.
[02:19.9] I think that that's really, really interesting.
[02:23.8] And it was actually a beautiful conversation that we had as a group.
[02:28.1] Talking about how you're reading this book that talks about censorship in other countries.
[02:33.8] And it's a different culture where books are banned and content is illicit.
[02:37.8] And it seems like this far away idea that impacts other places.
[02:42.8] And then it directly happens to us in a way that it wasn't done properly.
[02:49.8] It wasn't done according to process.
[02:51.8] And so it kind of brought the ideas in that other book really to the forefront.
[02:57.1] And it became a much more different experience.
[02:59.8] And then to kind of reread and then re-discuss that content after that had happened is something that I think a literary event like this, you never expect it to be that poignant.
[03:09.8] But it was kind of a neat experience, as frustrating as it was.
[03:15.2] Absolutely.
[03:17.0] What [do not use: interviewer]
[03:21.7] would you want the authors of these books to know about how their work is being received inside? [do not use: interviewer]
[03:26.8] Oh gosh, I would hope all of these authors of what I would want them to know about how the books are being received.
[03:33.8] That they're being received with so much gratitude and so much open-mindedness.
[03:42.3] There's been the ability of people from so many different personal backgrounds and cultural backgrounds to have conversations about the same things.
[03:52.8] And how different we all see them based on our own experiences.
[03:56.9] And I think it's really important for authors to know that their one piece of content
[04:01.9] can have so many different impacts based on the people that are looking at that content.
[04:06.8] And just the gratitude of being able to have meaningful content also be entertaining.
[04:14.0] That's really great.
[04:15.8] Absolutely.
[04:17.8] What has reading these books shown you that might surprise someone who thinks that books don't matter? [do not use: interviewer]
[04:27.6] What have they shown me that might surprise somebody who thinks books don't matter?
[04:34.6] Well, I would say the censorship example would be a really good thing.
[04:43.1] Something that people think that books don't matter.
[04:45.7] I think, like in the example of Adenon, being able to read content that was intentionally written from an indigenous perspective, following in more indigenous format.
[04:57.6] That gets across feelings and sensations and experiences that somebody who's talking about those experiences
[05:09.2] can never accurately portray.
[05:10.6] And I think that somebody who thinks books don't matter is really missing out on the opportunity to feel those experiences from the direct perspective of the people who are there.
[05:23.8] You can learn in a textbook about a certain culture all day long, but until you've sat down and read the content and had a conversation with somebody who is from that culture,
[05:32.8] you're just missing such a big array of colors on the color scheme, you know?
[05:39.4] Absolutely.
[05:39.8] That makes sense.
[05:42.5] Absolutely.
[05:43.0] Question, did you read all five books? [do not use: interviewer]
[05:45.0] All right.
[05:46.0] Still in that process.
[05:48.4] All right.
[05:49.4] I think we're good, because I think we're kicking off this event in five minutes. [do not use: off-topic]
[05:53.4] I'm going to ask for the microphone. [do not use: off-topic]
[05:55.4] Yeah, see, I would have ran off. [do not use: off-topic]
